title: Decoding the Right-to-Repair Debate
gist: The FY 2027 NDAA is the battleground over who controls technical data and IP to repair U.S. military equipment, with the House shifting the burden of proof to contractors and the Senate making government IP access a precondition for doing business with DOD. CSIS explains that a government purpose rights default could cut sustainment costs (about 70 percent of lifecycle cost) but would raise upfront contract prices and erode OEM aftermarket revenue, and lays out compromises such as no third-party transfer, data as a service, escrow and access agreements.

themes.theme: Stakes of IP control for OEM economics

insights.claim: Defense OEMs use control over technical data and IP to protect their technical edge and generate long-term revenue by maintaining government-owned systems they built.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Right-to-repair reform directly threatens high-margin sustainment revenue streams of defense primes.
insights.locator: Q2: How do IP rights affect

insights.claim: Sustainment accounts for roughly 70 percent of the total cost of major weapons systems, so a GPR default could let DOD use in-house repair or multiple vendors as lower-cost alternatives to OEMs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The sustainment pool is the largest share of program value, making aftermarket revenue the key exposure for primes.
insights.quote: sustainment accounts for roughly 70 percent of the total cost of major weapons systems and platforms
insights.locator: Q5: How would a GPR default

insights.claim: Senator Elizabeth Warren cited a helicopter control knob that cost the Army $47,000 to outsource for repair but could have been made in-house for $15, though CSIS notes it is unclear GPR would be required for that repair.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: High-profile cost anecdotes fuel political momentum for right-to-repair despite nuance.
insights.locator: Q5: How would a GPR default

insights.claim: A GPR default would raise contract prices significantly because contractors would charge higher upfront prices to offset lost IP control and forgone sustainment revenue.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reform may shift defense contractor revenue from aftermarket to upfront pricing rather than simply eliminating it.
insights.quote: It is also important to note that a GPR default would raise contract prices significantly.
insights.locator: It is also important to note

insights.claim: Industry's main objection to default GPR is the government's ability to share privately developed contractor IP with third parties, including potential competitors.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Third-party sharing provisions are the critical detail for whether reform benefits independent MRO providers at OEM expense.

themes.theme: Legislative state of play in the FY 2027 NDAA

insights.claim: The House FY 2027 NDAA shifts the burden of proof to contractors to justify tighter IP control, while the Senate version makes government IP access a precondition of doing business with DOD.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Senate approach is more aggressive; conference outcome will determine sustainment-revenue risk for primes.
insights.quote: The Senate bill goes a step further by making government IP access a precondition of doing business with the DOD.

insights.claim: The Goodlander-Harrigan House amendment would make government purpose rights the default IP framework in DOD contracts but apply only to future contracts, leaving existing equipment agreements untouched.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Existing program sustainment revenue is insulated; impact on OEMs would phase in with new contracts.
insights.quote: Importantly, this change would apply only to future contracts, leaving the IP terms negotiated under agreements for existing equipment untouched.

insights.claim: The House has passed its NDAA but the Senate has not brought its version to the floor, and no further action is expected until Congress returns from the midterm recess.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Right-to-repair resolution will be decided in the lame duck or later.

insights.claim: The FY 2026 NDAA compromise (Section 805) satisfied no one, and many lawmakers are unwilling to defer the right-to-repair issue further.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Raises the probability of substantive IP reform landing in the FY 2027 NDAA.
insights.quote: The FY 2026 NDAA compromise did not satisfy anyone

themes.theme: IP rights taxonomy and the OMIT/DMPD fault line

insights.claim: Government purpose rights let the government use, modify and share IP within government and release it to third parties for government purposes, and GPR typically converts to unlimited rights five years after the initial contract.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The five-year conversion means GPR effectively becomes unrestricted over a program's lifecycle.

insights.claim: Contractors must grant unlimited rights to operation, maintenance, installation and training (OMIT) data, but some OMIT data overlaps with detailed manufacturing and process data (DMPD), which is not automatically unlimited, creating major disputes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: How legislation treats DMPD determines whether OEMs lose manufacturing know-how, not just repair manuals.
insights.quote: a central question in the debate over any right-to-repair legislation will be how it applies to DMPD

insights.claim: A GAO report found DOD has consistently failed to acquire and track the IP and technical data rights needed to sustain its equipment, owing to poor long-term planning and lack of department-wide coordination.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Even without new law, DOD's weak data management limits its ability to break OEM sustainment lock-in.

insights.claim: DOD's Section 805 response, a database cataloging existing IP and data access, has frustrated lawmakers and industry with slow progress, and observers worry a centralized defense IP database poses security risks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Execution gaps may blunt near-term effects of right-to-repair mandates.

insights.claim: Data as a service, in which the government pays recurring subscription fees for IP usage, is promoted by industry as streamlining acquisition but criticized as burdening taxpayers and denying government needed control.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A DaaS outcome would convert OEM IP into recurring software-like revenue, a favorable result for primes.
insights.locator: Q8: What is the primary alternative

insights.claim: One compromise is a GPR default that bars government transfer of IP to third parties, letting DOD do organic repair while addressing industry's main concern, though GPR costs would remain.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: This path would favor DOD depots over third-party MRO competitors.
insights.locator: One option is to make GPR

insights.claim: Stakeholders have proposed that DOD plan vendor switches at key lifecycle points, such as using one vendor for production and another for sustainment, securing the needed IP up front.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Could open a distinct sustainment market for non-OEM contractors.

insights.claim: Industry argues sensitive software IP like source code should be treated as DMPD and excluded from unlimited OMIT rights, suggesting a separate software IP policy and hardware-specific approaches since munitions differ from ships and vehicles.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Software-heavy defense vendors have most to gain from a carve-out for source code.

insights.claim: Escrow agreements, where a neutral party releases IP to the government if a contractor goes bankrupt or ends support, and access agreements with NDAs offer middle-ground IP frameworks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: These tools could protect OEM IP while reducing government supplier-failure risk.
